content.text: Which of the following has both magnitude and direction?
Mass
Scalar
Speed
Vector
Start from the definitions: a scalar is a quantity described by magnitude alone, while a quantity that is incomplete unless a direction is also given is a vector. Test each option against that test.
One of the options is not a quantity at all - it is the name given to a whole class of quantities. The other three are all quantities, so only one of those three can satisfy the question.
D
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction is a vector; a quantity with magnitude only is a scalar. Test each option against that definition.

items: Mass: magnitude only, so it is a scalar - it cannot be the answer.
Scalar: this is the name of the class of quantities that have magnitude only, not a quantity that has a direction - it cannot be the answer.
Speed: this is the magnitude of velocity, i.e. the direction has been left out, so it is a scalar - it cannot be the answer.
Vector: by definition a quantity that has both magnitude and direction - this satisfies the question.

content.text: Force, velocity, displacement and acceleration are all vectors for the same reason, whereas mass, time, temperature, speed and volume are scalars.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: Which of the following methods would be suitable to manufacture PET polymer (polyethylene terephthalate) bottles?
Casting
Pressing
Stamping
Blow moulding

Think about how the bottle is actually made. A thin-walled hollow preform is produced first and is then inflated inside a matched metal mould, which is what gives a PET bottle its uniform wall thickness and sealed neck.
Check each other process: molten-material processes need a fluid melt, and sheet-forming processes leave an open shape with cut edges. Neither can produce a sealed, hollow, thin-walled container.
D

PET is a thermoplastic with a very high melt viscosity, so it cannot be cast or pressed into a bottle cavity. It is instead blow moulded: a thick-walled preform (a small closed tube) is heated until it softens, a high-pressure air blast is admitted inside it, and the preform inflates against the walls of a matched metal mould, taking the exact internal shape of the bottle. The plastic is stretched as it inflates, so the walls end up thin, uniform and stress-free, and the neck and base are sealed as part of the one operation.

items: Casting: needs a molten material that flows to fill a complex cavity; PET's melt is far too viscous, and a cast bottle would be heavy, thick-walled and brittle.
Pressing: a short forming stroke for sheet or simple bar sections - it cannot make a deep hollow sealed vessel.
Stamping: a sheet-metal forming operation that gives shallow, open shapes with sheared edges and flanges, not a hollow sealed bottle.
Blow moulding: inflates a heated preform against a mould cavity to form a sealed thin-walled bottle directly from the polymer - correct.
1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: A motor vehicle is travelling along a horizontal road. How does an increase in velocity affect its potential energy and kinetic energy?
: (A); Potential energy: Increases; Kinetic energy: Increases
: (B); Potential energy: Maintains; Kinetic energy: Increases
: (C); Potential energy: Increases; Kinetic energy: Decreases
: (D); Potential energy: Maintains; Kinetic energy: Decreases
Write both energies down before you read the options. The road is horizontal, so decide what happens to the height $h$ of the vehicle's centre of mass above the datum as it travels along.
The other energy depends on the square of the speed, not on the speed, so a rise in velocity always increases it. That eliminates every row that says kinetic energy decreases.
B
Gravitational potential energy of the vehicle:

The road is horizontal and the vehicle stays on the road surface, so its height $h$ above the datum does not change. The mass and $g$ are also unchanged, so the potential energy is maintained at a constant value. This eliminates the two rows that claim the potential energy increases.
Kinetic energy of the vehicle:

Because the velocity is squared, any increase in velocity increases the kinetic energy, so the two rows that claim kinetic energy decreases are also wrong. The remaining row - potential energy maintained, kinetic energy increasing - is the correct one.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: A pictorial view of a block is shown.

content.alt_text: Pictorial (isometric-style) view of a block with a sloping cut passing through it, with an arrow labelled 'Front View' pointing at the face that is the front.

content.text: Which option shows the front view of the block, looking in the direction of the arrow?

content.alt_text: Option A: three orthographic views of the block - a front view divided by two horizontal lines, a side view divided by two vertical lines, and a top view with a diagonal line rising from bottom left to top right.

Option B: three orthographic views of the block - a front view divided by two vertical lines, a side view divided by two vertical lines, and a top view with a diagonal line rising from bottom left to top right.

Option C: three orthographic views of the block - a front view divided by two horizontal lines, a side view divided by two horizontal lines, and a top view with a diagonal line falling from top left to bottom right.

Option D: three orthographic views of the block - a front view divided by two vertical lines, a top view with a diagonal line falling from top left to bottom right, and a side view divided by two vertical lines.

content.text: The arrow fixes the front view: work out which face it points at, then view the block square-on to that face. Do not assume the largest face in the pictorial is the front.

The sloping cut runs along the length of the block and climbs from one end to the other. Decide which end is higher, then check which way that makes the line lean in the front view; the two cut edges that run along the length will appear as straight lines parallel to the length in the plan and as vertical lines in the side view.
A

The front view arrow points at the large right-hand face of the block, so that face is the one seen in true shape in the front view. The sloping cut runs along the length of the block and rises from the near (left-hand) end towards the far (right-hand) end, so in the front view the cut appears as a single straight inclined line climbing from bottom left to top right.

The two edges of the cut run parallel to the length of the block. Projected onto the plan they stay parallel to the length, giving two horizontal lines; projected onto the side view the length direction is the viewing direction, so those same edges appear as two vertical lines.

items: Front view: one inclined line rising from bottom left to top right.
Plan (top) view: two lines parallel to the length of the block, i.e. horizontal.
Side view: the same two cut edges seen end-on, i.e. vertical.

content.text: Only one option combines the rising diagonal in the front view with horizontal lines in the plan and vertical lines in the side view. Options with a diagonal falling from top left put the high end of the cut on the wrong side of the front view, and options in which both other views have the same line orientation get one of the two elevation views wrong.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: The teeth on a steel sprocket need to be hard.

content.alt_text: Photograph of a steel sprocket with an arrow labelling one of the outer teeth 'Sprocket teeth'.

content.text: Which heat treatment process is most suitable for hardening the teeth?
Flame heating then air cooling
Flame heating then oven cooling
Induction heating then quenching
Induction heating then slow cooling

Case hardening needs two things: the heat must reach only the surface (so the tough core is not damaged), and the cooling must be fast enough to trap the hard structure instead of letting the atoms rearrange to the soft equilibrium form.
Rate the four options on those two points separately. Slow cooling - in air, in an oven or in a furnace - cannot produce a hard case, however well the part was heated.
C

Sprocket teeth must resist wear and contact forces, so they need a hard, wear-resistant surface layer while the core stays tough to resist impact. That means heating only the surface and then cooling fast enough to form martensite.

items: Flame heating then air cooling: the flame is aimed at the teeth, but air cooling is far too slow to form martensite, so the teeth only gain a slight surface toughening - not hard enough.
Flame heating then oven cooling: an oven is a slow cooling environment, so the austenite transforms to pearlite or spheroidite; the teeth are left soft, not hard.
Induction heating then quenching: the induced current heats only the surface of the teeth rapidly and locally without overheating the core, and quenching locks in a hard martensitic case - correct.
Induction heating then slow cooling: the heating is suitable but slow cooling cannot produce martensite, so no hard case is formed.

content.text: Induction heating is preferred over a flame because it is non-contact, can be applied to one tooth at a time as the sprocket is indexed, heats very rapidly and gives a clean, repeatable case depth.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

assets.alt_text: Photograph of a steel sprocket with an arrow labelling one of the outer teeth 'Sprocket teeth'.

content.text: Which process combines data and a carrier wave to form a television signal?
Compressing
Encryption
Modulation
Multiplexing
The data has to travel on a high-frequency carrier so it can be radiated from an aerial and received over long distances. Identify which process actually puts the information onto that carrier.

Two of the other options are about transmission efficiency (making the data smaller, or sharing one channel between several sources) and one is about security. None of those three alters the carrier itself.
C

Modulation is the process of varying a property of a high-frequency carrier wave - its amplitude, frequency or phase - in step with the information signal, so that the information and the carrier are combined into one signal that can be transmitted and received by an aerial.

items: Compressing: reduces the number of bits to be sent (so less bandwidth is needed); it does not put the data onto a carrier.
Encryption: encodes the data so that it cannot be read if intercepted; the encrypted result still has to be placed on a carrier afterwards.
Multiplexing: shares the one transmission channel between several separate signals (for example several TV channels); it does not combine data with a carrier.
Modulation: varies the carrier in step with the data, producing the combined signal - correct.

content.text: This is why the modulated signal cannot simply be sent down a wire: at the frequencies needed for long-distance transmission the modulated waveform carries the information and must be amplified and re-radiated as a radio wave.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: Which of the lever systems would require the least force at $X$ to balance the $100\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass?

content.alt_text: Option A: a bar on a triangular pivot with a 100 kg mass one division to the left of the pivot and the downward force X applied at the far right end of the bar.
Option B: a bar on a triangular pivot with the 100 kg mass resting directly on the pivot and the downward force X applied four divisions to the right of the pivot.
Option C: a bar on a triangular pivot with the 100 kg mass three divisions to the left of the pivot and the downward force X applied at the far right end of the bar.
Option D: a bar on a triangular pivot with the 100 kg mass two divisions to the left of the pivot and the downward force X applied near the right end of the bar.

content.text: Take moments about the pivot so that the pivot reaction disappears: $X \, d_{X} = W \, d_{W}$, with $W = 100 \times 9.81 = 981\,\mathrm{N}$. The bar is marked in equal divisions, so read both moment arms off directly in divisions - you do not need the length of the bar or its mass.

To get the least force you want the smallest possible moment arm for the weight AND the largest possible moment arm for $X$. Compare the ratio $d_{W}/d_{X}$ for all four arrangements and choose the smallest.
B
Equilibrium of moments about the pivot:
Reading the moment arms in bar divisions from the four diagrams:

items: A: mass 3 divisions left, $X$ 6 divisions right: $X = 981 \times \frac{3}{6} = 491\,\mathrm{N}$.
B: mass 1 division left, $X$ 3 divisions right: $X = 981 \times \frac{1}{3} = 327\,\mathrm{N}$.
C: mass 3 divisions left, $X$ 4 divisions right: $X = 981 \times \frac{3}{4} = 736\,\mathrm{N}$.
D: mass 3 divisions left, $X$ 3 divisions right: $X = 981 \times \frac{3}{3} = 981\,\mathrm{N}$.

content.text: The smallest force comes from the arrangement that combines the shortest moment arm for the 100 kg mass with the longest moment arm for $X$, which is the arrangement with the mass resting immediately beside the pivot and $X$ three divisions away. This is a second-class lever.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

Option C: a bar on a triangular pivot with the 100 kg mass three divisions to the left of the pivot and the downward force X applied at the far right end of the bar.

content.text: Which statement best describes the difference between cast iron and steel?
Steel contains more free graphite.
Cast iron has higher tensile strength.
Steel has higher compressive strength.
Cast iron has a higher percentage of carbon.
Both materials are iron-carbon alloys, so the comparison is made on the iron-carbon diagram. What single composition variable separates the cast iron region from the steel region?
Then check the properties in turn: free graphite flakes are what make grey cast iron grey and brittle, and they belong to the high-carbon side, not the low-carbon side.
D

Cast iron and steel are distinguished by carbon content. Grey cast iron contains roughly 2.5-4% carbon, much of it present as free graphite flakes - that is why it is grey in colour, weak in tension and not ductile. Steel is kept below about 2% carbon with the carbon combined in the structure, which is what makes steel hard, strong and ductile.

items: A is wrong: it is cast iron, not steel, that contains the free graphite.
B is wrong: grey cast iron has low tensile strength; steel is stronger in tension.
C is wrong: steel has higher compressive strength as well as higher tensile strength than grey cast iron.
D is correct: cast iron has the higher percentage of carbon.
1 mark: selects the correct option.

questions.notes: Key A verified against the original graph image. The stored alt text ('three positive half-sine humps with no negative half cycle') is misleading on its own, because the same description would fit half wave rectification; what distinguishes the two is that the humps are contiguous at zero with no flat gaps, which is the full wave case.

content.text: Which form of the AC to DC rectification process is shown by the graphs?

content.alt_text: Two voltage-against-time graphs. 'Before rectification' shows a sinusoidal AC waveform; 'After rectification' shows three positive half-sine humps with no negative half cycle.

content.text: Full wave
Half wave
Smooth full wave
Smooth half wave

Count the humps in the output against the cycles in the input, and look carefully at what happens at each zero crossing. Are the humps shoulder to shoulder, or is there a flat zero section the same width as each hump?

Decide how many half-cycles of the input each output hump represents. If every half-cycle is used there will be no flat sections; if only one half-cycle in two is used the gaps will be as wide as the humps.
A

The input shows one and a half cycles. The output shows three humps, each half a cycle wide, sitting shoulder to shoulder with no flat zero sections between them, so each output hump occupies both the positive and the negative half-cycle of the input. The negative half-cycles have therefore been turned upwards.

items: Full wave: both half-cycles are used, so the humps touch at zero and the ripple frequency is twice the input frequency - this is what is drawn.
Half wave: only the positive half-cycles pass, so there would be a flat zero section, as wide as each hump, between the humps - the gaps are absent here.
Smooth full wave and smooth half wave: a capacitor filter across the load would flatten the tops of the humps. The tops here are still fully curved, so no smoothing has been applied.

content.text: The output is therefore unsmoothed full wave rectification: the output is never negative and the ripple frequency is twice the supply frequency.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: The heat sink shown is used to conduct heat away from components.

content.alt_text: Photograph of a black extruded aluminium heat sink with parallel fins, with an arrow labelling it 'Heat sink'.

content.text: Which row of the table identifies a suitable material and manufacturing process for the heat sink?
Material: Steel; Manufacturing process: Rolling
Material: Nylon; Manufacturing process: Injection moulding
Material: Aluminium alloy; Manufacturing process: Die casting
Material: Ceramic; Manufacturing process: Compression moulding

A heat sink works by conduction, so the first requirement is a high thermal conductivity. Cross off any material that is a thermal insulator, or whose conductivity is much poorer than the common engineering metals.

For the process, ask whether it can form thin fins in a single operation as part of a complex moulded shape. Rolling makes sheet, and a moulding process can fill a cavity that already contains the fins.
C

Aluminium alloys have very high thermal conductivity for a metal, and they are light, which matters for equipment that has to be carried. Die casting is a suitable production process for a heat sink because the whole finned shape - base and fins - is cast in one operation in a single metal mould, with no machining of the fins required, and it is economical for the large batches typical of electronics.

items: Steel with rolling: steel conducts heat far less well than aluminium, and rolling produces flat sheet - it cannot form fins.
Nylon with injection moulding: nylon is a thermal insulator, so it would trap heat inside the component rather than conduct it away.
Aluminium alloy with die casting: excellent conductor plus a process that casts the fins in one piece - correct.
Ceramic with compression moulding: ceramic is a thermal insulator, used where electrical insulation is needed, not for moving heat away.
1 mark: selects the correct option.

assets.alt_text: Photograph of a black extruded aluminium heat sink with parallel fins, with an arrow labelling it 'Heat sink'.

content.text: Consider this logic circuit for turning a lamp on or off.

content.alt_text: Logic circuit: Switch 1 and Switch 2 feed a NOR gate (OR shape with an inversion bubble), whose output combines with Switch 3 in an AND gate; the AND gate output drives a lamp.

content.text: Which set of conditions will turn the lamp on?
Switch 1: Off; Switch 2: Off; Switch 3: Off
Switch 1: On; Switch 2: On; Switch 3: On
Switch 1: Off; Switch 2: Off; Switch 3: On
Switch 1: Off; Switch 2: On; Switch 3: On

Work from the switches towards the lamp, one gate at a time. The first gate is an OR gate with a bubble on its output - the bubble inverts, so this gate outputs a 1 only when both of its inputs are 0.
The second gate needs both of its inputs to be 1 at the same time before it drives the lamp. Work out what the first gate's output must be, then which single switch must be set.
C

The first gate is a NOR gate: it outputs 1 only when Switch 1 and Switch 2 are both off, and 0 in every other combination. The second gate is an AND gate, so the lamp is on only when the NOR output is 1 AND Switch 3 is on.

items: Switch 1 off, Switch 2 off, Switch 3 off: the NOR gate outputs 1, but the AND gate needs Switch 3 on as well, so the lamp stays off.
Switch 1 on, Switch 2 on, Switch 3 on: the NOR gate outputs 0 because its inputs are not both 0, so the lamp stays off.
Switch 1 off, Switch 2 off, Switch 3 on: the NOR gate outputs 1 and Switch 3 is on, so the AND gate outputs 1 and the lamp lights.
Switch 1 off, Switch 2 on, Switch 3 on: the NOR gate outputs 0 because one of its inputs is 1, so the lamp stays off.

content.text: So the lamp is turned on only when both switches feeding the NOR gate are off and the switch feeding the AND gate directly is on. (With both of the first two switches on the output is a logic 0, which is why that combination fails.)

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

assets.alt_text: Logic circuit: Switch 1 and Switch 2 feed a NOR gate (OR shape with an inversion bubble), whose output combines with Switch 3 in an AND gate; the AND gate output drives a lamp.

content.text: Each resistor in the diagrams below has a value of $10\,\Omega$.
Which combination of resistors provides a total resistance of $15\,\Omega$ between $X$ and $Y$?

content.alt_text: Option A: three resistors in series connected between terminals X and Y.
Option B: three resistors in parallel connected between terminals X and Y.
Option C: two resistors in series forming the upper branch and one resistor forming the lower branch, the two branches in parallel between X and Y.
Option D: one resistor in series with a parallel pair of two resistors, connected between terminals X and Y.

content.text: Reduce each network one step at a time: series resistors add directly, and parallel resistors combine with $\frac{1}{R_{t}} = \frac{1}{R_{1}} + \frac{1}{R_{2}}$.

Then look for the arrangement that mixes the two rules. A single resistor in series with a parallel pair gives a total between the single value and the sum of the pair - check whether that combination lands on the required value.
D
Reduce each option with the series and parallel rules:

items: A: three in series, $R_{t} = 10 + 10 + 10 = 30\,\Omega$.
B: three in parallel, $\frac{1}{R_{t}} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10}$, so $R_{t} = 3.33\,\Omega$.
C: two in series in the upper branch in parallel with one in the lower branch, $R_{t} = \frac{20 \times 10}{20 + 10} = 6.67\,\Omega$.
D: one in series with two in parallel, $R_{t} = 10 + \frac{10 \times 10}{10 + 10} = 10 + 5 = 15\,\Omega$.

content.text: Only the single resistor in series with the parallel pair gives the required 15 $\Omega$ between X and Y; the other three networks give 30 $\Omega$, 3.33 $\Omega$ and 6.67 $\Omega$.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

Option B: three resistors in parallel connected between terminals X and Y.
Option C: two resistors in series forming the upper branch and one resistor forming the lower branch, the two branches in parallel between X and Y.
Option D: one resistor in series with a parallel pair of two resistors, connected between terminals X and Y.

questions.notes: Source defect: options B ('Vertical to the supporting surface') and D ('Perpendicular to the supporting surface') are effectively the same statement. D is keyed because 'perpendicular to' is the correct engineering term and 'vertical to' is not standard usage; a marker should accept either letter but the item is ambiguous as printed.

content.text: In which direction does a reaction force act at a roller support?
Parallel to the supporting surface
Vertical to the supporting surface
Horizontal to the supporting surface
Perpendicular to the supporting surface
Ask what the support is physically able to resist. A roller sits on a smooth surface that it is free to slide along, so no friction (force along the surface) can be generated.

If friction is not available, the only force the support can generate is the one pushing straight into the contacting surface. This is what makes a roller a single-reaction support, unlike a pin, which can resist two components.
D

A roller support rests on a smooth surface and can slide freely along it. Because no friction is available, the support cannot develop any force along the surface, so its reaction must act normal to (perpendicular to) the contacting surface. This is why a roller is drawn as a one-direction support in a free-body diagram.

items: A (parallel to the surface) and C (horizontal to the surface) both require friction along the surface, which a roller cannot provide.

B ('vertical to the supporting surface') is not correct terminology: whether a reaction is vertical or horizontal depends on how the surface is drawn, whereas the general rule is normal to the contacting surface.
D (perpendicular to the supporting surface) states the general rule and is correct for any orientation of the supporting surface.
1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: The image shows one end of an electrical spark plug used in an internal combustion engine. The component labelled $M$ is the terminal that carries the high-tension current to the centre electrode.
Which combination of properties would the component labelled $M$ need to have?
Electrical resistivity and machinability
Electrical conductivity and machinability
Electrical resistivity and temperature stability
Electrical conductivity and temperature stability

Two decisions are needed. First, does M have to PASS the high-tension current or BLOCK it - that fixes the electrical property. Second, what is the environment like where M sits, which fixes the second property.

The component sits at the top of a spark plug in an engine bay, so it is repeatedly cycled through high temperature. Also note that the terminal is a bought-out casting or forging, so think about whether being easy to machine could ever be a design requirement for it.
C
Read M off the figure. The arrow points to the glazed ceramic insulator at the top of the spark plug, not to the metal terminal lug that clips onto the high-tension lead.

The first property follows from the job the ceramic does. The insulator has to stop the high-tension voltage at the top of the plug leaking away through the body to earth, which means it must have high electrical resistivity, that is very low conductivity. A conductive insulator would short the plug out and no spark could jump the gap at all.

The second property follows from where it sits. The insulator runs in one short length from the cold air outside the engine bay down to the combustion chamber, so it is cycled steeply in temperature and has to keep its properties unchanged while it does - it must not soften, crack or lose its insulating ability when it heats. That is temperature stability.

Machinability appears in options A and B and is never a requirement for a bought-out insulator, which is not machined in manufacture, so both are eliminated. Option D gets the second property right but reverses the first: a high conductivity would defeat the insulating job. Option C is the only row that satisfies both requirements, so the answer is C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C (electrical resistivity and temperature stability), recognising that the ceramic insulator must resist leakage of the high-tension current to earth and must survive being cycled through a wide temperature range

Option B: pie chart of aircraft materials in which composite is the largest sector (half the circle), with aluminium alloy, titanium and steel as smaller sectors and a small 'Other' sector.
Option C: pie chart of aircraft materials in which composite is the largest sector, followed by steel, titanium and a small aluminium alloy sector, with a small 'Other' sector.
Option D: pie chart of aircraft materials in which aluminium alloy is the largest sector, followed by titanium, composite and steel, with a small 'Other' sector.

content.text: Think about a current-generation wide-body jet rather than a classic airliner. What single material now makes up roughly half the structure by mass, and where do aluminium alloy, titanium and steel sit in the order after it?

You are looking for one material filling about half the pie, one clear second, then two small slices and a very small 'other'. Read the sector sizes, not just the order - two of the options have a plausible order but the wrong second-largest material.
B

In new large passenger aircraft such as the Boeing 787 and the Airbus A350, carbon-fibre reinforced polymer is the primary structural material, at roughly 50% by mass. Aluminium alloy is the next largest share (retained for the fuselage skin, wing stringers and much of the empennage), with smaller shares of titanium (high-strength areas, gear and engine components) and steel (landing gear, fasteners, some primary structure), plus a small 'other' sector.

items: A makes aluminium alloy the largest sector - that describes older airliner designs, not new large passenger aircraft.
B has composite as the largest sector, aluminium alloy clearly second, then titanium and steel, and a small 'other' - correct.
C makes steel the second largest material, which is wrong; steel is one of the smaller shares.
D makes aluminium alloy the largest sector and titanium the second, which is wrong on both counts.

content.text: The shift to composites is driven by their very high specific stiffness and specific strength, which allow a lower operating empty weight and less fuel burnt over the aircraft's life.

content.text: Which of the following could cause fatigue cracking in a metal?
A static tensile load
A substantial shock load
A high compression load
A cyclically applied load
Fatigue is a failure mechanism that needs a large number of load applications to build up damage. Ask which of the loadings repeats many times at a stress well below the material's strength.

Keep fatigue separate from overload: a single large load, however big, causes yielding or immediate fracture, and a constant high compressive load causes crushing or buckling instead of a fatigue crack.
D

Fatigue is progressive damage caused by repeated loading. Each cycle produces a tiny amount of plastic deformation at a surface defect or stress concentration, and the crack grows a little further every cycle until the remaining section fails - often at a stress well below the yield strength and with no visible warning.

items: A static tensile load: the load is constant, so there is no cycling; it causes elastic deformation or permanent yielding, not fatigue.
A substantial shock load: a single overload event, which causes immediate ductile or brittle fracture - the opposite of progressive fatigue.
A high compression load: constant; it can cause crushing, yielding or buckling of a slender member but will not initiate a fatigue crack.
A cyclically applied load: repeated varying stress initiates and propagates a fatigue crack - correct.

content.text: Fatigue is why components such as shafts, springs, welds and aircraft structures are designed with a fatigue safety factor, and why their endurance limit is a specified property.

items: 1 mark: selects the correct option.

content.text: What are TWO advantages of using the powder forming (sintering) process to manufacture a self-lubricating bearing?
Low material waste and high density
High porosity and low material waste
Low density and high tensile strength
High quality surface finish and high tensile strength

Powder metallurgy presses metal powder into a die and then sinters it. Ask what happens to the material that a machined part would have had to be machined away as swarf, and how dense the finished component is compared with the loose powder it started as.

Reject any pair that includes high porosity or low density as an advantage - porosity is a weakness of sintered parts, not a benefit. Also ask what sintering does to tensile strength compared with a machined or cast component.
A

In powder forming the powder is pressed into a die to give a 'green' compact close to its final shape, then heated so the particles fuse. Because the shape is produced by pressing rather than by removing material, almost none of the metal is machined away, which gives very low material waste; and because sintering consolidates the compact, the finished part has a high density for a sintered product. Both are standard advantages of the process.

items: A: low material waste and high density - both are genuine advantages of powder forming - correct.
B: high porosity is a disadvantage. The self-lubricating bearing relies on a controlled amount of porosity, but porosity is not an advantage of the manufacturing process itself.
C: low density and high tensile strength are the opposite of what powder forming gives.
D: sintered bearings are not chosen for a high-quality surface finish or for high tensile strength - those belong to machined parts.

content.text: Because the die cavity gives the final shape, complex features such as the oil grooves and radial flutes of a self-lubricating bearing are formed directly and the part often needs no further machining.

The 500 N/m UDL over 8 m is a total of 4 kN acting at mid-span, so the total load is 3 + 4 + 7 = 14 kN. Taking moments about the left support:

The three parts test three different skills: identifying components and their functions, explaining a technological influence, and producing a technical drawing. Do not let the style of one answer leak into another.

The element in series with the tuned circuit can conduct on part of each cycle only; the element in shunt with the loudspeaker provides a low-impedance path that diverts something away from the loudspeaker. Ask what would reach the loudspeaker if it were not diverted.

content.text: Name the components labelled $A$ and $B$ and outline each component's function in this circuit.
Start from where each component sits in the circuit. The component in series with the tuned circuit can conduct on one half of the cycle only — that behaviour is what tells you its name and its job.

The component in shunt (parallel) with the loudspeaker provides a low-impedance path that diverts part of the signal away from the loudspeaker. Ask what would still be reaching the loudspeaker if that component were not there.
Each mark pair is a name plus a function, so give them in that order and do not describe the function before naming the component.
Component $A$: a diode; it rectifies the AC signal.
Component $B$: a capacitor; it filters out the carrier wave.
Component $A$ is the diode in series with the tuned circuit. It conducts on one half cycle only, so it rectifies the AC signal to a unidirectional (DC) signal.
Component $B$ is the shunt capacitor across the output. Together with the load it bypasses the remaining high-frequency carrier component, smoothing the signal before it drives the loudspeaker.

content.text: How have semi-conductors influenced the design of modern telecommunications products?
The question asks about the design of the product, so answer with what the designer can now do or make better — not with how a semiconductor behaves electrically.

Miniaturisation of components (smaller devices), lower power use (more efficient), faster processing speeds, increased scale of integration, more robust construction and better in-service performance.

content.text: Contrast the key features of fixed and mobile telephone systems.
Build the answer as matched pairs — one feature of the fixed system with the opposite feature of the mobile system beside it — rather than as two separate descriptions that never meet.
The strongest contrast is the transmission medium itself; interference, dropout, bandwidth, security and the locations that can be served all follow from it, so start there and derive the rest.

content.text: Outline how an analogue signal is digitised using *sampling* and *quantising*.
The analogue wave is continuous in two independent ways — in time and in amplitude — and digitising removes each continuity by a different mechanism.
Decide which of the two terms deals with the intervals between readings and which deals with the number of discrete levels a reading may take, and say what each one produces on the lower graph.

An analogue signal is continuously variable and must be converted to a range of set values to produce a digital signal. Sampling is taking a measurement at specified time intervals, while quantising is assigning one of a set range of values at each time interval.
Sampling: the amplitude of the continuously varying analogue signal is measured at a series of equally spaced time intervals, so the signal is represented by a set of discrete samples.
Quantising: each sample amplitude is then assigned the nearest value from a fixed set of permitted levels, producing the stepped digital signal shown.

items: 4 marks: outlines the conversion process using sampling AND quantising.
2–3 marks: outlines features of the conversion process and/or sampling and/or quantising.
1 mark: identifies a feature of the conversion process.

content.text: The following parts refer to light aircraft: the choice of propulsion system, the control adjustments that vary lift, a wind tunnel test of an aerofoil, and non-destructive testing of aircraft components.

Each part asks a different thing: (a) which engine suits which aircraft and why; (b) which control adjustments change the lift force; (c) resolve a wind tunnel resultant into lift and drag; (d) describe a non-destructive test and its advantage.

For (a) the justification has to be functional - speed and range for one class of aircraft, short field length and simple maintenance for the other. Naming the engine type alone does not earn the justification mark.
For (c) the 350 N is the resultant of lift and drag, not the lift itself, so it has to be resolved into two perpendicular components before any ratio is formed.

3 marks: part (b) — Outline TWO control adjustments that can be made to vary the lift force acting on an aircraft during flight.

content.text: Identify a suitable propulsion system for each aircraft and justify your choice.
Identify the engine type for each aircraft from the drawings: look for jet intakes and a jet exhaust on one, and a nose-mounted propeller on the other.
Then justify: what does each class of aircraft actually need from its engine? Consider speed and range for one of them, and runway length, purchase cost and maintenance sophistication for the other.
A justification that only says 'jets are fast' is incomplete - tie the engine type to a specific operating requirement of that class of aircraft.
The business aircraft has a jet engine and the recreational aircraft has a propeller-driven piston engine.

Jet engines suit business aircraft because they give greater speed and longer range; propeller engines suit recreational aircraft because they need shorter runways and less sophisticated maintenance systems.

The business aircraft is a twin-engine jet; the recreational aircraft is a single-engine propeller aircraft. Justification should link the propulsion type to the operating requirement of each aircraft class.

items: 3 marks: identifies TWO propulsion systems and provides a reason why each is appropriate.
2 marks: identifies a propulsion system and provides a valid explanation of why it is appropriate, OR identifies a suitable propulsion system for each aircraft.
1 mark: identifies a relevant propulsion system.

content.text: Outline TWO control adjustments that can be made to vary the lift force acting on an aircraft during flight.
Lift depends on three things: the angle the wing is set at, how fast the wing is moving through the air, and how much wing area there is. Each of the three can be adjusted.
One of them is limited: beyond a maximum angle of attack of about $15^{\circ}$ the flow separates from the wing and lift is lost, so angle of attack cannot simply be increased indefinitely.
Aim to name TWO distinct adjustments, and for each one say which of the three quantities it changes.
Adjusting the angle of attack, which changes the amount of air the wing forces down; the maximum angle of attack is about $15^{\circ}$.

Adjusting the thrust (power) supplied by the aeroplane engines, which changes the amount of air the wing forces down; an increase in power increases lift but requires a compensating adjustment of angle of attack. Wing spoilers may also be used to dump lift, and the wing surface area may be adjusted.
Two acceptable adjustments are the angle of attack and the thrust/power setting; spoilers to dump lift and changes to wing surface area are also accepted.

items: 3 marks: outlines TWO relevant adjustments that can be made to vary the lift force.
2 marks: outlines ONE relevant adjustment that can be made to vary the lift force, OR identifies TWO relevant adjustments.
1 mark: shows a basic understanding of lift force.

content.text: This test produced a resultant force of $350\,\mathrm{N}$ at an angle of $10^{\circ}$ to the lift axis.
Calculate the lift to drag ratio.
The 350 N is the resultant of the lift and the drag, inclined at $10^{\circ}$ to the lift axis - it is not the lift itself.
Resolve the resultant: the component along the lift axis is the lift, and the component perpendicular to it is the drag.
Form the ratio as lift divided by drag, then quote it with the smaller quantity written first. Watch the degree mode on your calculator.

content.text: Outline the ultrasonic testing process and its advantages for use in testing aircraft components.
Two things are required: how the test actually works, and what makes it worth using on aircraft components.
For the process, think in terms of a sound wave being sent into the component and something coming back. A flaw in the material changes both what returns and how quickly it returns.
For the advantages, consider what a maintenance technician does NOT have to do to an aircraft under this test, compared with a test that requires the part to be removed or cut open.

Ultrasonic inspection operates on the principle of transmitted and reflected high-frequency sound waves. It measures the change in the velocity of sound waves passing through a substance and produces an 'echo' if there is a flaw in the material being tested. It is used for aircraft maintenance because it can test parts while they are still in place.

A high-frequency sound wave is sent into the component; the time taken for the wave to travel and for an echo to return is measured. A flaw reflects part of the wave early, so the shortened return time reveals the defect. The main advantage is that the component does not have to be dismantled for the test.

items: 4 marks: outlines the testing process and provides relevant advantages.
2–3 marks: outlines the testing process and/or the advantages.
1 mark: identifies a relevant feature.

content.text: An engineering team consists of a civil engineer, an electrical engineer and an environmental engineer. They have been contracted by a local council to manage the design and construction of a five metre long pedestrian bridge across a narrow creek in a public park.
Outline how each of these engineers would contribute to the successful completion of this project.
Take one engineer at a time and ask what that discipline is responsible for between the design brief and the structure being signed off and opened to the public.

Look for the four kinds of contribution NESA rewards here: drawings, calculations, supervision and safety on site, and statutory paperwork such as an Environmental Impact Statement prepared for the consenting authority.
Civil engineer: structural design drawing for the bridge; structural and cost calculations for the bridge; ensuring a hazard free working environment; site management.
Electrical engineer: design and cost electrical systems for the bridge; supervise installations on the bridge; final safety testing and certification.

Environmental engineer: prepare an Environmental Impact Statement for the council/consenting authority; conduct environmental audits; minimise the environmental impact of construction of the bridge; site rehabilitation.
Each specialist contributes in their own discipline:

items: Civil engineer — structural design drawings, structural and cost calculations, safe work site management.
Electrical engineer — design and costing of electrical systems, supervision of installation, final safety testing and certification.
Environmental engineer — Environmental Impact Statement for the consenting authority, environmental audits, minimising construction impact, site rehabilitation.

6–7 marks: outlines the responsibilities that at least two of the engineering specialists should exercise in the design and construction of the new structure.
4–5 marks: outlines the responsibilities that at least two of the engineering specialists should exercise in the design or construction of the new structure.
2–3 marks: outlines the responsibilities of engineers and/or requirements of the project.
